newsitem.title: FRANCE: Helmut Schmidt says Tietmeyer against EMU - paper.
newsitem.headline: Helmut Schmidt says Tietmeyer against EMU - paper.

text.p: Former German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt said in an interview published on Friday that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer and Bundesbank Chief Economist Otmar Issing were campaigning against a single European currency.
"The gentlemen of the Bundesbank believe that a single currency must be made on their terms or not at all," Schmidt is quoted as saying in an interview with daily Liberation.
"I continue to believe that the officials of the Bundesbank are campaigning against a single currency. Not all of them. But certainly Issing or Tietmeyer," Schmidt said.

Schmidt said he was pleased the European Union agreement on a budget discipline pact had not stuck to Germany's demand for automatic fines in all cases when countries run public deficits greater than three percent of gross domestic product.

Asked if he was grateful for French insistence on softening the terms of the so-called "stability pact" he said German Finance Minister Theo Waigel had been wrong to take such a strict position on the pact.

"It is not that it was 'softened', the German position was absolutely not imposed. The French were right and reason carried the day. The German finance minister and the Bundesbank were mistaken about Germany's true interests," he said.
He pointed out that if Germany's vision of the stability pact were in force in 1996 Germany would have had to pay "several billion marks" of penalties.
Schmidt said the mark and the franc were overvalued.
"Yes, the two currencies are overvalued compared to the world's other currencies," Schmidt said.

"The consequences of the strong mark ideology can be seen in a simple difference: In Germany, where unemployment is over 10 percent, the discount rate at which banks refinance themselves at the central bank is 2.5 percent. In Japan, where unemployment is half as high, the central bank's money costs 0.5 percent," he said.
He also blamed the German government for the resistance to a single currency among German people and said there would be no referendum in Germany on the issue.
"The Maastricht treaty was ratified by the Bundestag. There will not be a referendum in Germany. The people don't have to be convinced anymore," Schmidt said.
"The government has itself to blame if all it has done for the last two years is talk constantly about the stability of the mark and done nothing to cut unemployment."
